transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I keep rechecking and fixing how I look before I go out or get on camera, and it’s starting to make me late and stressed all the time. My sister actually noticed how much it was affecting me and encouraged me to come in and get some help.

When you are checking and fixing how you look, is it mainly because you have intrusive fears or doubts that something bad will happen if you do not, or is it mainly because you feel a specific part of your appearance is flawed or ugly?

It's definitely because I feel like certain parts of my face look flawed and ugly, not because I'm worried about something bad happening. I get really hyper-focused on how crooked my jaw looks and how bad my skin is. I end up constantly checking the mirror and adjusting myself just to try to feel "less ugly" before anyone sees me.
Do you spend a lot of time on other repetitive behaviors or mental rituals too, like checking, counting, cleaning, or repeating thoughts, even when they are not about your appearance?

No, I don't really do any of those other things like counting or cleaning, and I don't have rituals unrelated to my looks. My checking and fixing behaviors are strictly focused on my appearance and trying to get ready to go out.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were [F45.2, F42.8], but the interview now strongly favors F45.2 because the repetitive behaviors are clearly driven by preoccupation with perceived appearance defects (jaw, skin) and are limited to mirror checking and fixing looks. F42.8 is less likely because there are no intrusive fears of harm, no broader obsessions, and no other compulsions or rituals outside appearance-focused behaviors.

Based on the interview, the main new concern is repetitive rechecking and fixing of appearance that is time-consuming and causing distress and impairment, which raises an obsessive-compulsive spectrum condition. However, the focus is specifically on perceived appearance defects and getting on camera, so a body-image related condition is also plausible. A somatic preoccupation disorder remains in the differential because the behavior is centered on appearance concerns, but there is not yet enough evidence about a fixed belief in having a defect versus intrusive obsessions/compulsions. More history is needed to distinguish these possibilities, so the list includes all three for now.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has persistent preoccupation with perceived facial defects (crooked jaw, bad skin) with repetitive mirror checking and fixing behaviors, causing lateness, stress, and social/functional interference. The behaviors are driven by appearance concerns rather than fear of harm and are not better explained by broader obsessive-compulsive rituals. This is most consistent with body dysmorphic disorder.
